quote: Do you guys have, like is there a, double money credit or anything like that, a military credit or anything that, the double money, you?
stewart_read: The customer asks a direct, specific question about a military/double-money discount. The rep never answers it — instead of admitting uncertainty or confirming/denying the specific program, she redirects to a different, generic incentive (bill swap, no down payment). This is a dodge-and-redirect, not a transparent admission of not knowing.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have correctly judged that no such military discount exists and simply offered the real incentives instead of confirming a negative — but she never actually says 'we don't have that specific program' so the customer's literal question is left unanswered.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to either confirm or deny the specific program asked about before pivoting to other incentives — an unanswered direct question can read as evasive even when the redirect is well-intentioned.

quote: Well, so, actually, our company, we do have this one incentive going on. We're doing what's called a bill swap program.
stewart_read: In response to a discount question, the rep volunteers program mechanics (bill swap, fixed rate, no down payment, no upfront cost) before any qualification or bill data has been gathered — explaining the offer rather than creating curiosity about the customer's own numbers.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as simply answering a direct customer question about incentives, which is reasonable rep behavior rather than a scope violation.
coaching_implication: When customers ask about discounts/incentives early, a shorter acknowledgment plus a bridge back to qualifying questions keeps curiosity focused on the customer's own bill rather than on company programs.

quote: I'm just closing out on March 23. So I'm just gonna kind of stop in that. I I don't own, like, as of right now, but on March 23, I should own it.
stewart_read: The customer is proactively planning ahead for solar before he even owns the home — asking for an estimate in advance so he can install immediately upon closing. This is a highly motivated, forward-planning lead, not a soft or reluctant one.
coaching_implication: Manager should note this lead's motivation level is high; the rep's callback commitment should be treated as a priority follow-up, not a routine one, given the customer's proactive planning.

quote: So we, unfortunately, would have to just wait until you close on the March 23.
stewart_read: This is a non-standard scenario — a soon-to-be homeowner rather than a current one — that the rep handles by deferring the entire estimate/design process to the closing date rather than attempting any workaround.
alternative_hypothesis: A reactive read would say the rep gave up too easily on gathering bill/usage data now so the estimate could be ready faster after closing; but the rep's own statement that 'my design team, unfortunately, cannot create the estimate until you are' (a homeowner) suggests this is a hard procedural gate, not a rep choice.
coaching_implication: Confirm with Kenny whether any pre-close data (utility bill, usage) can be gathered now to speed up the March 23 estimate, since the rep did not attempt this.

quote: And so I will reach back out on March 23 just to get that estimate to you. Okay?
stewart_read: The rep commits to a callback date but never locks a specific time, nor confirms contact method, nor gets a verbal handshake ('is that fair?') — the close is procedurally loose even though the date itself is concrete.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the hard ownership gate, a specific time may be premature since the rep doesn't yet know her own schedule three-plus weeks out — this could be a reasonable simplification rather than a true gap.
coaching_implication: Even on a deferred callback, anchor a rough time window (morning/afternoon) and get an explicit 'does that work for you' confirmation to increase the odds of a live pickup on March 23.
